lesson.title: Measuring the Sloshing: The Volt-Ampere-Reactive (VAR)
lesson.summary: The VAR (volt-ampere-reactive) is the unit used to measure reactive power, the portion of AC power that oscillates between source and load without ever being consumed, and it quantifies exactly the burden that power factor correction is designed to cancel.
lesson.body:
Reactive power is the piece of AC power that inductors and capacitors trade back and forth with the source every cycle without ever converting it into heat, light, or motion. An inductor's magnetic field builds up and collapses, a capacitor's electric field charges and discharges, and each time that happens energy flows out of the source and then flows right back in a quarter cycle later. Nothing is used up, but current still has to flow to make it happen, and that current still has to be supplied by generators, carried by wires, and handled by transformers. VAR is the unit that measures the rate of that sloshing exchange, named for volt-ampere-reactive to distinguish it clearly from the watt, which measures power that is actually consumed.

Reactive power is computed as Q = V x I x sin(theta), where V and I are rms voltage and current and theta is the phase angle between them, mirroring the real power formula P = V x I x cos(theta) but swapping cosine for sine. The two formulas share the same V and I because they are just two different projections of the same phasor relationship, one onto the in-phase axis (real power) and one onto the quadrature axis (reactive power).

Take a load drawing 120 V rms and 10 A rms with a lagging power factor of 0.8, meaning cos(theta) = 0.8 and theta = 36.87 degrees. Since 0.8 and 0.6 form the familiar 3-4-5 triangle, sin(theta) = sqrt(1 - 0.8^2) = sqrt(1 - 0.64) = sqrt(0.36) = 0.6. The real power is P = V x I x cos(theta) = 120 x 10 x 0.8 = 960 W, and the reactive power is Q = V x I x sin(theta) = 120 x 10 x 0.6 = 720 VAR.

It is worth confirming these numbers are consistent with the apparent power. Apparent power is S = V x I = 120 x 10 = 1,200 VA, and the power triangle relation S^2 = P^2 + Q^2 should hold exactly: 960^2 + 720^2 = 921,600 + 518,400 = 1,440,000, and 1,200^2 = 1,440,000 as well, so the triangle closes perfectly. This is the same 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 240 (3 x 240 = 720, 4 x 240 = 960, 5 x 240 = 1,200), which is a handy pattern to recognize when checking power calculations by hand.

VAR ratings show up constantly on real equipment: a capacitor bank might be rated 500 kVAR, meaning it can supply 500,000 VAR of reactive power to cancel an equivalent amount of lagging VAR from inductive loads, exactly the mechanism used in power factor correction. Whenever you see VAR on a nameplate or a utility bill, it refers to this non-working, oscillating power, always kept as a separate accounting line from the watts that the equipment is actually paying to consume.

The sign of Q also carries information that magnitude alone does not. By convention, an inductive load draws positive VAR and is described as having a lagging power factor, because its current lags its voltage. A capacitive load draws negative VAR relative to that same convention and is described as leading, since its current leads its voltage. That sign is exactly why a capacitor placed in parallel with an inductive load can cancel reactive power instead of adding to it: the two Q values have opposite signs and partially subtract, which is the entire arithmetic underlying power factor correction and is worth keeping straight whenever you see VAR values combined across a circuit with mixed inductive and capacitive elements.
